 Dalvin Brown , The Wall Street Journal 6 min read 3 Nov 2026, 06:45 AM IST 
 Summary
 Feed one side of a family fight into a chatbot and you might get the legal answer you want to see, but it won’t necessarily fly with the judge. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Steven Benmor, a Toronto family lawyer, recently drafted a prenuptial agreement the way he said his client asked. Then the client emailed him a 13-part list of revisions nearly as long as the prenup.
 Some revisions went so deep into the weeds, Benmor said, that no human could have come up with them. Benmor knew his client had turned to an artificial intelligence chatbot. And he knew that taking the time to explain why the chatbot was mistaken would require charging his client extra.
 His mantra: “Don’t spend money unduly by asking a human expert to enter into a debate with a robot expert.”
 It was hardly the first time this had happened to Benmor. Family lawyers, who handle everything from prenups to divorces and custody fights, say many of their clients are now showing up with pages of legal advice that look like the result of ChatGPT or other chatbots.
 In a spring survey of 133 lawyers at Cordell & Cordell, a national family-law firm, 80% said clients had sent them correspondence, draft pleadings or strategy suggestions they believed were generated with AI.
 People ask chatbots for everything these days, including financial advice and medical diagnoses. But family law isn’t a place where they shine, lawyers say. Feed one side of a family fight into a chatbot and you might get the legal answer you want to see, even if it isn’t one that will necessarily fly with the judge.
 Divorcing partners turn to them anyway. Money is often tight for people when a marriage comes apart, and hiring a lawyer takes time. A chatbot answers right away, even in the middle of the night.
 Logan Burns used ChatGPT for legal advice and ended up having to apologize to the judge. Burns, a 35-year-old pastor and roofing salesman in LaGrange, Ga., paid a Georgia lawyer a $2,500 retainer when his marriage came apart last year. The couple called off the divorce and tried to reconcile, and his wife took the children to stay with family in Montana. When the reconciliation failed, the custody fight landed there, where a lawyer wanted $7,000. He paid $19.99 a month for the chatbot instead.
 “It was doing the job of a lawyer, or at least a paralegal,” he said.
 ChatGPT pointed him to a rule that generally lets a state decide custody once a child has lived there for six months. His children had been in Montana for less than that. Burns wanted the case moved to Georgia.
 So he wrote the judge a letter arguing that the court had improperly taken over his children’s case. The judge brought it up in court. “You technically don’t have jurisdiction,” Burns recalled telling the judge. The judge sternly told him that wasn’t how it worked. The rule has exceptions: Courts can step in during emergencies, and Burns had filed an emergency request himself.
 “Your Honor, I’m not accusing you of anything,” he recalled saying. “ChatGPT gave me the baseline information. But it doesn’t give you the interpretation of law.”
 He has temporary custody of his children, though the case is ongoing. “Thank you, AI,” Burns said.
 Damien Charlotin, an adjunct professor at UC Law San Francisco who tracks AI-generated errors in court cases, has counted 148 family-law rulings in which judges flagged fake citations or other apparent AI mistakes. More than 100 came this year.
 Chatbots also tend to take one side’s word at face value, even though two sides often disagree on facts in family law. The owner of an online wellness company had agreed in his divorce to pay hefty spousal support, based on what the business was earning. Years later, taking far less money out of the business, he asked a chatbot whether a judge would cut his payments. The bot told him he had an easy win.
 The chatbot never asked to see his financial statements, or his spending, which hadn’t shrunk with his income. It “simply accepted our client’s narrative regarding his finances,” said Hossein Berenji, a Los Angeles family lawyer whose firm later took the case.
 Relying on the chatbot’s advice, he hired a lawyer and persuaded the attorney to follow the chatbot’s strategy. In late 2024, the lawyer asked the court to reduce the support, attaching some company records. The other side’s lawyer used those same records to argue his income hadn’t really fallen, and about a year later the judge agreed. The man blamed his lawyer, not the chatbot, and switched to Berenji’s firm. “It took us a while to convince him to move away from what AI was advising him to do,” Berenji said.
 The firm brought in a forensic accountant, who found what the first filing had left out: A lot of the company’s products had spoiled while the business was still paying its overhead, Berenji said. Sales were big. What was left for his client wasn’t.
 At a recent hearing, a judge tentatively agreed his finances had changed and put his support payments on hold for now.
 What the chatbot called an easy win took two law firms and nearly two years.
 Everything the man paid his first lawyer was “basically money thrown down the drain,” and he likely overpaid spousal support the whole time, Berenji said.

 The filings appeared to be written by AI, Kamal said. “It was scaring my client.”

docs.text:
Explainer 
 Mint Primer | From SBI to Binance: why even the biggest financial platforms are under cyber siege
 Shelley Singh 3 min read 2 Nov 2026, 01:25 PM IST 
 Summary
 Today’s financial ecosystems are interconnected, making them vulnerable at multiple points. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Recent incidents involving Binance and the State Bank of India show that no financial institution is immune to cyber threats. As banking and crypto platforms lean on sophisticated technologies, hackers are not far behind. They are targeting customer data, exposing vulnerabilities that can fuel fraud, identity theft and financial crime. Mint explains. 
 What happened at Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange? 
 In the biggest crypto hack in history, cyber criminals siphoned $6.3 billion from Binance platforms in just 20 minutes on 29 October. The hackers manipulated internal systems linked to transactions, approvals and withdrawals at the world’s largest crypto exchange. 
 On 1 November, the US Federal Bureau of Investigation traced the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korea hacking group that converted the stolen assets primarily into Ethereum. Binance said about 95% of the stolen assets have since been covered. 
 Binance, founded in China in 2017, allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets . It had 335 million registered users globally and about $162.8 billion in assets in 2025.
 How was State Bank of India (SBI) targeted recently? 
 SBI, India’s largest bank, disclosed on 21 October a suspected data breach after receiving alerts from CERT-In, the Defence Cyber Agency and its threat intelligence provider. About 375,000 records were found circulating on the dark web. 
 SBI identified 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information. The exposed details reportedly included names, mobile numbers, dates of birth, email addresses, residential addresses and loan-related metadata. 
 Core banking operations were not affected, neither was any money stolen. However, such information can be exploited for phishing, impersonation and social-engineering attacks targeting customers. An independent cybersecurity investigation is underway. 
 What system vulnerabilities lead to such incidents? 
 Today’s financial ecosystems are interconnected, making them vulnerable at multiple points. Weak passwords, compromised employee credentials, phishing attacks, insecure application programming interfaces, third-party vendor risks and misconfigured cloud systems are among common weak links. 
 Cybercriminals often exploit human error rather than sophisticated technical flaws. Financial institutions also manage massive amounts of customer data across numerous systems, creating a large attack surface. Legacy infrastructure coexisting with newer digital and AI platforms adds to the complexity and security challenge.
 In many cases, stolen data originates not from a direct breach but from malware infections, credential theft or poorly secured partner ecosystems. 
 Will there be more cyberattacks in future? 
 Just days before the hack, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao wrote on X: “No crypto wallet is 100% safe. No tech is 100% secure.” 
 As financial services become more digital and AI-powered, cyberattacks are expected to increase. Criminal groups now use AI tools to scale attacks.
 To strengthen security, banks, fintech firms and crypto exchanges must adopt a ‘zero-trust’ architecture, continuously verify users and devices, enforce multi-factor authentication, encrypt sensitive data, monitor networks in real time and conduct frequent security audits. 
 Stronger security across networks is equally critical. Employee training, customer awareness, threat intelligence sharing and rapid incident response capabilities are essential components of cyber defence. 
 Will quantum computing make financial ecosystems more vulnerable to attacks by cyber criminals? What can users, banks do? 
 Powerful quantum machines may be able to break some of today's widely used encryption standards. While such capabilities are not yet commercially available at scale, regulators and cybersecurity experts are already preparing for ‘post-quantum’ security. 
 Banks should start testing quantum-resistant algorithms and plan migration strategies. Financial institutions will need crypto-agility, enabling them to replace encryption methods quickly as standards evolve. 
 The SBI and Binance episodes show that cybersecurity is no longer merely an IT issue. It is a systemic financial-risk issue. As digital finance expands, resilience—not just innovation—will determine which institutions retain customer trust.

docs.title: India’s market slump: Here's why palliatives aren't enough to attract foreign investors
docs.text:
Opinion 
 India’s market slump: Here's why palliatives aren't enough to attract foreign investors
 Mint Editorial Board 3 min read 2 Nov 2026, 07:30 AM IST 
 Summary
 Changes in the capital gains tax alone won’t bring back foreign investors. Policymakers need to push through difficult reforms to drive the growth of high-value globally competitive firms. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Indian equities rank among the worst performing emerging market assets today, despite the rebound in October. The benchmark Nifty 50 index has fallen 12% this year (17% in dollar terms), Bloomberg data shows. 
 Among major emerging markets, only Indonesian equities have fared worse, with the benchmark IDX Composite index falling 42% this year (46% in dollar terms), following a warning from Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) that Indonesia might lose its emerging market status. 
 The slump in Indian markets is partly because of large-scale selling by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs), who have pulled out about ₹ 3 trillion from Indian equity markets so far this year, a decadal high. The outflows have weakened the rupee, and in turn lowered the dollar returns foreign investors earn from Indian equities. 
 There are several contending explanations for the slump. One thesis points to the lack of artificial intelligence (AI) firms in the country. Since investors have poured gazillions of dollars into AI firms and AI-linked sectors, India has lost out. As the AI trade weakens, India would stand to gain, according to this thesis. 
 A second thesis emphasizes geopolitical tensions that have pushed up commodity prices. As a large commodity importer, India has been hit harder than the rest. Related to this, rising inflation and bond yields in the US have narrowed the spread between US and emerging market assets, weakening fund flows to emerging markets. 
 As geopolitical tensions subside and the global commodity cycle cools, India would be back in favour, the proponents of this thesis argue. 
 A third thesis emphasizes the lack of innovation among large Indian firms. Without the promise of sustained earnings growth, Indian stocks would remain unattractive to foreign investors, Bernstein Research analysts Venugopal Garre and Nikhil Arela wrote in a note to clients a few weeks ago. 
 If the AI trade weakens, or oil prices decline, foreign capital might return temporarily. But sustained flows would depend on “whether India can create new engines of competitiveness, innovation and global relevance,” they wrote.
 The new firms emerging in areas such as space, defence, semiconductors and deep-tech are currently too small to attract global capital at scale, the duo argued.
 None of these explanations suggest that changes in capital gains taxes can bring back foreign funds. To be sure, there are distortions in our capital tax structure, and this should be addressed, as this newspaper has argued earlier (see ‘ LTCG and STT: Optimize taxes that investors pay, ’ 19 October). Rationalizing capital gains taxes would help foreign and domestic investors choose more appropriate assets for themselves. But they are not a quick-fix to stem capital outflows. 
 The repricing of stocks in the current slump could itself rekindle interest in Indian markets. It is worth noting that foreign investors have invested heavily in initial public offerings in the recent past even as they have avoided overpriced stocks in the secondary market. 
 Policymakers should focus on difficult reforms that could catalyse the growth of high-value globally competitive firms in the country. These firms should be free to dedicate their resources to develop innovative products rather than expend them in managing the bureaucracy.

 The Mint Editorial Board is a panel of editorial writers with expertise across diverse domains of relevance to the newspaper’s opinion readers. docs.title: America’s Gulf allies prepare for new round of strikes on Iran—and the blowback
docs.text:
Global 
 America’s Gulf allies prepare for new round of strikes on Iran—and the blowback
 Summer Said , Benoit Faucon , The Wall Street Journal 6 min read 3 Nov 2026, 06:49 AM IST 
 Summary
 The risks are growing as diplomatic efforts remain stalled and Iran threatens unrestrained retaliation. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 DUBAI—America’s Gulf allies are steeling themselves for a heavy U.S. bombardment of Iran that they expect to trigger a vicious cycle of retaliation against their own economic and civilian infrastructure as early as this week.
 Their concerns are heightened by a lack of progress in the various efforts to reach a negotiated end to the conflict while the U.S. and Iran are threatening especially ferocious fighting if the conflict resurges.
 President Trump has been leaning toward a large postelection attack that could target Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, but hasn’t decided whether to go ahead, The Wall Street Journal has reported. Iranian officials said over the weekend their response to any attack would be unrestrained.
 “The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can,” Trump said Sunday at a rally in Iowa ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. “But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer.”
 Governments including Qatar and the United Arab Emirates were running security drills—including at airports—and attendees at a major energy conference in Abu Dhabi were cutting short their stays on advice from their governments. Schools in the capital of Saudi Arabia, which is also under fire from the Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, will remain online this week. Dutch and Belgian embassies in the region warned Thursday that security conditions could deteriorate quickly in the region.
 Anwar Gargash, senior foreign-policy adviser to the U.A.E.’s president, said at a security conference over the weekend that the country hopes the diplomatic efforts will pan out, but is “braced for the worst.”
 Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said at the same conference that a new round of escalation would be more destructive and that efforts in the coming days or weeks would be critical to heading it off.
 The U.S. military has prepared options for attacks—restocking munitions in the region and beefing up defenses, including by moving troops out of vulnerable bases and sending another Patriot antimissile system to Israel.
 Trump has ramped up threats before, most recently in late July, only to back down in hopes of a negotiated deal.
 Tehran politely welcomed a letter sent in late October by Vice President JD Vance seeking to open talks with Iran’s top national security official, Mohsen Rezaei. But so far it hasn’t responded formally to Vance’s request to discuss Iran’s nuclear program and hasn’t agreed to a meeting, mediators between the two sides said.
 Talks in the main diplomatic channel, mediated by Qatar, are stuck on whether the U.S. or Iran should be the first to make concessions to move talks along, the mediators said.
 Gulf states are growing alarmed that they may face more destructive Iranian attacks than at the height of the war in March. Iran lacks the firepower to blunt U.S. and Israeli airstrikes and has adopted a strategy of quickly raising the stakes in any exchange by attacking its more vulnerable neighbors across the Persian Gulf.
 Iran has threatened publicly and in private diplomatic communications to attack a broad array of U.S. and Gulf targets in the region in response to any U.S. strike.
 “There is no world in which a short and sharp strike by the U.S. will be absorbed by Iran,” said Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at U.S. think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies. “An intense infrastructure-based targeting campaign by Washington is likely to beget one by Tehran against U.S. partners.”
 Some Arab states have warned Iran they could retaliate individually or collectively if Tehran targets their infrastructure, the mediators said. The U.A.E. carried out strikes on Iran over the spring, but other Gulf states largely sat out the fighting.
 Gulf states are scrambling to come up with new formulas to break the diplomatic deadlock.
 Qatari mediators, who had previously proposed a seven-day period in which the U.S. and Iran would lift their restrictions on traffic in Hormuz to build confidence for further talks, traveled to Tehran on Friday with a revised plan that would cut the confidence-building period to two days, Iran says.
 Under one of the proposals floated by Qatar, the U.S. would loosen its naval blockade if Iran halted attacks on shipping in the strait for an agreed number of days, the mediators and an Iranian official said. Iran would then allow international nuclear inspectors back into the country and start a discussion on its stockpile of enriched uranium within a few days, they said. Once inspections are completed, the U.S. would lift some sanctions, they said.
 But Qatar has had difficulty nailing down an agreement. The U.S. is reluctant to lift its blockade before clear progress on nuclear issues, fearing Iran will buy time by rushing bottled-up oil shipments out of the Gulf, mediators said. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman said Monday there had been no discussion of nuclear issues.
 Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi returned to Tehran from Doha on Sunday after talks failed to yield enough progress to trigger a visit from U.S. negotiators, mediators said.
 Still, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran was willing to continue talks. “We are trying to solve the problem through dialogue. In this regard, the supreme leader of the revolution has also given the government certain powers,” he said without elaborating, state-run IRNA news agency reported Monday.
 Last week got off to an unpromising st

docs.title: US pushes to restore Russian gas sales to Europe via Ukraine
docs.text:
Global 
 US pushes to restore Russian gas sales to Europe via Ukraine
 Yaroslav Trofimov , Drew Hinshaw , Joe Parkinson , The Wall Street Journal 6 min read 2 Nov 2026, 08:35 AM IST 
 Summary
 The idea is intended to unlock an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv but it faces resistance in European capitals. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The U.S. is backing a quick resumption of Russian natural-gas sales to Europe via pipelines running through Moscow’s wartime enemy—Ukraine—as part of negotiations aimed at securing an energy ceasefire ahead of the coming winter, according to U.S., European and Ukrainian officials.
 The idea, broached by U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff during trips to Moscow and Kyiv in September, would involve selling Russian gas via a U.S. intermediary to circumvent European sanctions—and could create a lucrative opportunity for American investors, people who attended the discussions said.
 Under current European Union legislation, all purchases of Russian natural gas must be phased out by the end of 2027. Leaders of Europe’s biggest nations have said that they have no interest in restoring their dependence on energy supplies from a country they view as their top strategic threat.
 The plan was put on the back burner last month after Ukraine unilaterally stopped striking Russian refineries under pressure from President Trump. Kyiv paused strikes on Russian refineries for almost two weeks as Russia continued pounding Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and as Moscow began shipping diesel to the U.S. The U.S. shifted focus to the possibility of a more substantial peace agreement.
 Kyiv, however, resumed its air campaign on Friday, launching three attacks on three major Russian refineries in the past three days. This has brought new urgency to the pursuit of a more comprehensive energy ceasefire ahead of three-way peace negotiations that are planned between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine for mid-November in Abu Dhabi. Russia so far has rebuffed American attempts to strike such a deal.
 In the view of U.S. negotiators, a Russian comeback to the European natural-gas market would create a powerful incentive for President Vladimir Putin to agree. Using the Soviet-era pipeline network that runs to Europe via Ukraine from the Urengoi gas fields in Siberia would also provide Kyiv with badly needed revenue from transit fees.
 White House officials proposed that Russia deposit proceeds earned from these gas sales to Europe into an escrow account in a third-party jurisdiction, so that the Kremlin won’t use the money to finance its war, said a senior U.S. official. They have tried to sell the idea to European leaders as a way to lower energy prices ahead of a winter when Europe’s gas reserves have reached their lowest seasonal level in several years.
 Such pressure represents a complete about-turn from Trump’s first administration. Back then, Trump repeatedly chastised German Chancellor Angela Merkel for building the Nord Stream 2 pipeline from Russia. He warned that Nord Stream 2 would make Germany “captive to Russia,” and, in late 2019, imposed sanctions on it.
 Just over two years later, Russia—its military funded by energy-export revenues—invaded Ukraine, betting that Europe wouldn’t react because of its heavy economic dependence on Moscow.
 The war, however, prompted the Europeans to view dependence on Russian natural gas a strategic vulnerability to a hostile power they no longer trust. The EU has passed legislation sharply curtailing Russian gas imports and outlawing them altogether by the end of next year. The current official European position is that the EU won’t resume purchases of Russian gas even after a full peace agreement with Russia, let alone as part of a tenuous energy ceasefire that allows Putin to continue the war and provides funding for his military.
 EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen, in an interview with a Hungarian newspaper in October that his office has confirmed, said the ban on Russian gas imports should be permanent.
 “I certainly would not trust Russia. Even if there were peace tomorrow, which we all hope for,” he said.
 The Trump administration is wagering that European resistance will prove to be less rigid than meets the eye.
 But in private, some senior European officials are more blunt. A senior Nordic official said the idea of resuming Russian gas purchases goes against everything the Europeans stand for, while a senior official from a large European nation compared it to former British leader Neville Chamberlain sacrificing Czechoslovakia to Hitler in exchange for business deals.
 The U.S., for its part, now sees an eventual reopening of Nord Stream as a potentially important component of a larger deal, not just to end the war in Ukraine but to resolve Russia’s longstanding friction with America’s European allies. Merkel’s mistake, a senior U.S. official said, was to pursue the pipeline without first working toward a wider security arrangement with Russia that Moscow could feel comfortable with.
 Russia and Germany built the first Nord Stream pipeline to bypass the networks running via Ukraine in 2011. docs.text:
Global 
 Trump’s Monday speech at high-drama reflecting pool is an apt end to midterms
 Damian Paletta , The Wall Street Journal 4 min read 2 Nov 2026, 05:54 PM IST 
 Summary
 All eyes will be on Washington, D.C., and the Lincoln Memorial, where President Trump will give his closing remarks this afternoon. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Good morning. President Trump canceled and uncanceled rallies.
 He hosted a jungle-themed Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago.
 He praised an estranged Democrat while eviscerating one of his former lawyers, referring to her behavior as “totally obnoxious and outrageous.”
 He commented on the posterior of multiple people and attacked Bill Maher in a 1,300-word Truth Social post.
 On Sunday, he alleged multiple people had broken election laws and appeared to call for new investigations.
 That was all part of the closing message.
 As the 2026 midterms bumble and stumble and fumble to a close, all eyes will be on Washington, D.C., and the Lincoln Memorial, where Trump will give his closing remarks at the Reflecting Pool, which has already had its fair share of drama this year.
 He won’t be on the campaign trail, in Texas or Kansas or Michigan, where big Senate races are coming down to the wire.
 Instead, he’ll be back at the site of one of his many controversies this year. Remember the charges and dropped charges and the blowup with Jeanine Pirro? And this isn’t far from the Kennedy Center, the site of another controversy; and also not far from where he wants to build a Triumphal Arch, another controversy; and quite frankly not far from where he wants to build a new golf course, another controversy. Detect a theme?
 Will it end where it began? Is he stronger than he looks? Only voters can determine.
 Back in September in Dallas (2,000 news cycles ago), Trump implored Republicans to act like he was on the ballot. He believed that he alone can drive turnout for Republicans. Perhaps true. But he can also drive turnout for Democrats. The 2018 midterm elections were the high-water mark for voter turnout, and that’s when Democrats seized back control of the House.
 Even though Democrats have had their share of fiascos in the past week (Alaska and Michigan, to name a few), there are many signs that the election could come down to Trump’s low approval rating, the Iran War quagmire and high prices. If that’s the case, then there isn’t much many House and Senate Republican candidates can do. There’s only one messenger who can take that on, and that’s what he will attempt to do Monday at the Lincoln Memorial at 2 p.m. ET.
 This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.
 People and Policies I’m Watching
 Midterms sprint to the finish: As candidates make their final pitches to voters, follow the latest developments here.
 Trump’s Monday: Trump will take part in tele-rallies in the morning, then speak at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool at 2 p.m. He will later take part in more tele-rallies.
 What I’m Following
 David Jolly pitches political civility in bid to flip Florida. In the Florida governor’s race, Democrat David Jolly has made political decency a central part of his campaign during one of the nastiest midterm seasons in recent memory. Facing off against Republican Byron Donalds—a congressman and staunch Trump ally—Jolly is waging a campaign aimed at voters who want a less divisive, more civil kind of politics.
 Battle continues for the future of the Democratic Party. Allies of the party’s leaders privately say that an insurgent left-wing has unnecessarily sucked time and money into races that should have been easier for Democrats, to the detriment of other candidates. Progressives say the party’s establishment isn’t doing everything possible to help them win, according to people familiar with the conversations. Both factions want a Democratic Senate. Whatever the outcome, Tuesday’s results are poised to accelerate an internecine battle for the future of the party.
 How Rep. Haley Stevens turned on Abdul El-Sayed. Rep. Haley Stevens stunned Democrats on Sunday when she withdrew her endorsement for her Democratic primary opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, and backed Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race. Her reversal sparked condemnations from Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and from her own state’s Democratic Party, who said she was no longer welcome as a member. By Sunday evening, she had become a pariah in her own party.
 What Else Is Happening
 Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, a rising star in the Democratic Party, suffered a stroke on Saturday.
 A namesake challenge to Sen. Dan Sullivan seemed harmless—until the candidate vanished and federal agents started knocking on doors.
 The U.S. is backing a quick resumption of Russian natural-gas sales to Europe via pipelines running through Moscow’s wartime enemy—Ukraine.

 About Me
 I’m Damian Paletta, The Wall Street Journal’s Washington coverage chief. I’ve covered Washington for 22 years as a reporter and editor. I’ve covered the White House, Congress, national security, the federal budget, economics and multiple market meltdowns.

docs.title: November 2026 income tax calendar: Check key deadlines for TDS payments, tax certificates and ITR filing
docs.text:
Here are the key November deadlines to keep track of. Tax deducted or collected at source (TDS/TCS) during October 2026 must be deposited with the Central Government by 7 November. This applies to deductors and collectors responsible for depositing tax deducted or collected during the previous month. Another compliance requirement due on this date relates to uploading declarations received in Form 127 under the Income-tax Rules, 2026. This form is a declaration furnished by a buyer to the seller under Section 394 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, where the buyer seeks to avoid tax deduction at source (TDS). Deductors must issue TDS certificates in Form 132 by 14 November for tax deducted during September 2026 under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Form No 132 is a TDS certificate issued for tax deducted on specified transactions, including rent payments, transfers of immovable property, payments for technical services, and transfers of Virtual Digital Assets (VDAs). Deductors must issue this certificate within 15 days from the due date for filing the corresponding challan-cum-statement in Form No 141. 15 November is an important compliance date for deductors and collectors. 21 November is an important date for businesses and taxpayers covered by specified audit requirements. The deadline for filing ITR for Assessment Year (AY) 2026–27 has been extended from 31 October to 21 November 2026 for taxpayers whose accounts are required to be audited. These taxpayers were required to submit their tax audit reports by 21 October 2026. 30 November is the deadline for filing ITR for AY 2026–27 for taxpayers required to furnish a report under Section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961. This includes taxpayers engaged in international or domestic transactions subject to transfer pricing provisions. Additionally, Form 141 must be furnished by 30 November for specified TDS deductions made during October 2026. Form 141 is a consolidated challan-cum-statement for reporting TDS deductions on transactions such as transfers of immovable property, rent payments, payments to contractors or professionals by individuals and Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs) and transfers of Virtual Digital Assets (VDAs). docs.text:
Global 
 Companies have a solution for the skilled trade shortage: more women
 Te-Ping Chen , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 2 Nov 2026, 06:42 AM IST 
 Summary
 As women make inroads in male-dominated fields, firms look to improve jobsite culture. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Sammy Cossairt has tried call center work, waiting tables and hoisting concrete. She prefers hoisting concrete.
 The 36-year-old tower crane operator in Nashville, Tenn., who works 12-hour shifts, helps lift and move rebar and buckets of concrete from a perch often hundreds of feet in the air. This isn’t what she envisioned when she received a liberal arts associate degree more than a decade ago, but after nearly a decade on the job, she feels at home in her crane.
 “I’m out in the sun, making my mark on the world,” said Cossairt, who makes $120,000 a year. “I think more women would love to get in and make men’s money doing this work, if they only knew.”
 The skilled trades have long been a boy’s club. But more women are breaking in, drawn by well-paying jobs that are in high demand. To keep them coming, many companies are courting women like Cossairt through new benefits and perks, including paid maternity leave and more flexibility. They are also trying to create a more welcoming work environment while cracking down on off-color jokes and catcalls on male-dominated jobsites.
 The federal government tracks female participation in fields such as construction, and installation and repair, which includes jobs such as plumbers, carpenters and auto technicians. As of last year, women made up about 4.4% of those workers. But they have made mostly steady gains, with that figure rising from 2.9% a decade earlier.
 At Universal Technical Institute’s campus in Exton, Pa., career services director Katie Yurick said women are enrolling partly because the industry has grown more tech-infused. Automotive technicians can hook up cars to computers for diagnosis, and plenty of in-demand jobs—such as welding and electrical work—can trade as much on brains and attention to detail as brawn.
 “These jobs aren’t even dirty jobs anymore,” said Yurick, adding that she has also heard from employers who say they are trying to hire women, believing they possess high maturity levels and are detail-oriented.
 UTI’s student body, which spans 17 campuses across the U.S., is now 8% female, quadruple what it was five years ago. In some areas, such as collision repair and auto refinishing, that figure is even higher, at 19%.
 “Our industry needs this workforce,” said Maja Ericksen, executive vice president at construction company Mortenson, which in 2024 began offering 12 weeks of paid leave for birth mothers in its skilled workforce. More than 10% of Mortenson’s skilled workforce is now female, up from 7% a decade ago.
 “There aren’t too many careers you feel are AI-proof, and being in the skilled trades is one that isn’t going away,” Ericksen said.
 Women have broadly outperformed men in the labor market in recent years. This partly reflects booming growth in fields that traditionally employ more women, such as healthcare and social assistance, while women also are making inroads in traditionally male-dominated jobs.
 Kym Gardner, 39, a project engineer in Charlotte, N.C., said that as a child, she never thought about working in the field. Her mother was a teacher, her father a computer analyst. “No one really talked about it, it wasn’t considered to be a career,” she said. “The expectation was to go to college.”
 But in high school, she grew interested in architecture, found a construction mentorship program and quickly fell in love with seeing buildings rise from the ground up. Now the mother of three children, including a 5-month-old, starts her days on site and works remotely in the afternoons—flexibility she said helps give her peace of mind and ensures she doesn’t have to sacrifice her caregiving duties.
 Her company, Turner Construction, is growing fast and needs all the workers it can get, said president Abrar Sheriff. The company hit $29 billion in revenue last year and expects around $35 billion this year, fueled in part by work on data centers. More worker flexibility, including creature comforts such as heated and cooled bathrooms with running water on worksites, or regularly cleaned breakrooms, are part of the pitch.
 “We need more people to come into our industry,” Sheriff said.
 Elsewhere, construction company Skanska has taken steps such as ensuring female employees have correctly sized gloves, helmets and work boots, rather than forcing them to make do with male-sized gear. Deila Ray, who spent a decade as a pipe welder and now teaches the trade in high school, said she had to shrink her own gloves with fire when she started in the industry.
 Skanska this year also started mandating inclusivity for all its team leaders, encouraging them to be more aware of different workers’ needs, said Ayesha Adams, who joined Skanska in 2023 as its inaugural director of culture and engagement.
 “You can get people all day, but how do you keep them here?” Adams said.
 Some states are trying to make work in the trades more accommodating for women. Both Washington and Illinois, for example, have in the last few years passed laws requiring nursing rooms for mothers on construction sites, as well as refrigerators to store breast milk, flexible break schedules and access to water for cleaning.
 Construction companies are also tackling another issue: workplace harassment. At Turner, senior leaders there get on a call within four hours of any incident being reported. In one recent case in Texas, a subcontractor’s entire project crew of around a dozen men were replaced when that company couldn’t identify who had written derogatory graffiti about female employees, said Sheriff, Turner’s president.

News 
 Emirates NBD charts next phase of India expansion after RBL deal
 Priyamvada C 9 min read 2 Nov 2026, 11:50 AM IST 
 Summary
 Emirates NBD is leveraging its acquisition of RBL Bank to tap into India's growing middle-class and affluent segments, scale digital banking synergies across the UAE-India corridor and expand its footprint through strategic bolt-on acquisitions and venture investments. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 A little over a year after its $2.7 billion majority acquisition of RBL Bank, UAE-based Emirates NBD is looking to deepen its India presence, including scouting for minority investments in Indian startups through its venture capital platform. 
 Neeraj Makin, group head of strategy, analytics and venture capital at Emirates NBD and an RBL Bank board member, discusses the rationale of the acquisition, the bank’s India ambitions and its next phase of growth in an interview to Mint . Edited excerpts: 
 What makes India an attractive market for Gulf-based capital today? 
 India is one of the fastest-growing major economies in the world, with a population of approximately 1.4-1.5 billion. 
 From a UAE perspective, the relationship with India is particularly significant. Indians account for about 35-40% of the UAE’s population, and the two countries have built a strong economic partnership, supported by robust trade agreements. India is the UAE’s second-largest trading partner, while the UAE is India’s third largest. 
 This strong bilateral relationship is also translating into growing investment flows, with several UAE-based institutions and businesses exploring or expanding their presence in India or vice versa. Recent transactions and investments by players such as ADIA, Mubadala and IHC are further indicators of the growing confidence and long-term interest in the Indian opportunity. 
 What gave you the confidence to undertake the RBL transaction? 
 When evaluating the India opportunity… one of the key exercises we undertook was to study China’s growth story and the corresponding growth of its banks. We looked at where some of its leading banks stood in 2000 and how they had grown over the following two decades. 
 Some Indian banks today have asset bases of $50-100 billion, while their Chinese counterparts, which were at a similar scale in 2000, have since grown nearly 17-20x to $1 trillion to $1.3 trillion. This gave us a sense of the potential ahead and the possibility of 15-20x growth over the long term. 
 What does the country need to support that growth? 
 India’s GDP grew by around 7-8% in FY26, ahead of several estimates. Sustaining this growth requires a strong banking system and significant capital. This capital can come either from the government or private investors. Unlike China, where the government played a major role in funding growth, we see India relying increasingly on domestic and foreign private capital, including investors like us.
 Take us through how you approached India as your next area of deployment… 
 India should not be viewed as a homogeneous market, but rather through the lens of its distinct customer segments. While the top 0.5% represents the high-net-worth segment, our primary focus is the approximately 350 million people spanning the middle class to the affluent segment, which represents our natural sweet spot as a bank. 
 Beyond the growth of India’s middle class, we also looked at a range of other indicators, including purchasing power parity. According to third-party research, an estimated 50 million people in India today have incomes equivalent to $50,000 or more on a PPP basis, with this segment projected to grow to around 130-150 million over the next five to seven years. 
 Our India expansion journey actually began with another asset before we entered the RBL process. One thing that has always been consistent in our strategy, as reflected in our past acquisitions, is that we prefer to acquire businesses with control. Most of our previous acquisitions have been 100% buyouts. In India, that was however not possible. 
 At the same time, we recognize our responsibility to support broader economic growth and meet priority-sector lending requirements. We therefore intended to build a balanced franchise that serves our target customers while fulfilling our regulatory obligations and contributing meaningfully to India’s growth story. 
 What were the discussions in the lead up to the RBL transaction? 
 Historically, foreign interest in India’s banking sector was fairly limited. However, as the segment grew over the last five to seven years, the country saw greater interest from international strategics. 
 Earlier, most foreign investment came from private equity funds, which typically have fixed investment horizons. From a regulator’s perspective, this may raise concerns about the long-term stability of banks when these investors eventually exit. Our approach was different. We wanted to invest for the long term, and that was the message we communicated to the government. 
 Why RBL? How are you thinking of scaling the asset today? 
 RBL’s scale was one of the factors that made it particularly attractive to us. It gave us the opportunity to enter India in a measured way while retaining the flexibility to shape and grow the bank around our strategy. The initial capital commitment was also more manageable compared with some of the other opportunities we considered. Another important consideration was that our investment was going directly into the bank, providing fresh capital that can now be used to support and accelerate RBL’s growth. 
 When we first engaged with RBL, it had around 550 branches. Today, that number has grown to approximately 620-630. We are also discussing further expansion in markets where we see strong remittance flows with links from significant Indian diaspora, as well as opportunities to grow our commercia

docs.title: Maharashtra Charity Commissioner did not propose rule that froze Tata Trusts board
docs.text:
News 
 Maharashtra Charity Commissioner did not propose rule that froze Tata Trusts board
 Nehal Chaliawala , Varun Sood , Satish John 5 min read 3 Nov 2026, 05:40 AM IST 
 Summary
 An RTI response shows the regulator sent no proposal for the amendment that has paralysed Sir Ratan Tata Trust and contributed to a deadlock at Tata Sons. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 MUMBAI/BENGALURU: The Maharashtra Charity Commissioner did not propose the rule that has paralysed Sir Ratan Tata Trust (SRTT), the second-largest shareholder in Tata Sons, for nearly six months. The rule that resulted in the suspension of the trust’s board proceedings was introduced by the state government and invoked by the commissioner on 15 May this year, as per the public trusts regulator's office.
 In response to a Mint query under the Right to Information Act, 2005, the charity commissioner's office said it had sent no proposal to the state's Law and Judiciary Department regarding the Maharashtra Public Trusts (Amendment) Ordinance, 2025.
 Promulgated on 1 September 2025, the ordinance capped the number of perpetual trustees at one-fourth of a public trust’s total board strength, where its trust deed does not specifically provide for their appointment. The earlier law did not prescribe such a numerical cap.
 “In the above context, it is hereby informed that no proposal has been submitted by the Charity Commissioner, State of Maharashtra to the state’s Department of Law and Justice,” the commissioner's office said on 15 October in a response to the Mint RTI query.
 “Therefore, the records in this regard are not available in this office,” it said in a letter drafted in Marathi, which Mint has translated.
 The charity commissioner's office reiterated its position in a subsequent email to Mint on Monday, adding: “However, the deliberations were made in the Law and Judiciary Department.”
 The amendment has prevented SRTT from conducting board proceedings, contributed to a deadlock at Tata Sons and stalled the company's annual general meeting (AGM), complicating efforts to resolve a leadership dispute.
 The state's Law and Judiciary Department, which issued the ordinance, has declined to provide details of how the amendment was drafted. Asked for copies of Cabinet proposals, stakeholder representations and lobbying records, and inter-departmental correspondence relating to the ordinance, it said work on the file was “in progress at the Government level” and the information could not be provided “at present”.
 The ordinance made several changes to the law governing public trusts. The state legislature ratified it in December 2025 as the Maharashtra Public Trusts (Second Amendment) Act, 2025.
 Experts said it was unusual to amend a law without a proposal from the regulatory body responsible for implementing it.
 “Generally, the introduction of law or any amendments to existing laws are introduced with consultation of the regulatory body (state or central) of that law because ultimately, such regulatory body ensures the effective implementation of the law or its amendments,” said Gaurav Pingle, partner at Forefront Legal Consulting LLP.
 “In case of amendments, there could be reporting or disclosure requirements which would require the overview of the concerned regulatory body,” he said.
 The charity commissioner's office, however, functions under the state's Law and Judiciary Department. This differs from the institutional structure of federal regulators such as the Reserve Bank of India and the Securities and Exchange Board of India, whose offices are outside government ministries, even though the Centre appoints their heads and can issue policy directions.
 Emails sent to Maharashtra's Law and Judiciary Department seeking comment went unanswered until press time.
 SRTT under a freeze 
 The amendment became central to the dispute on 28 April, when Tata Trusts vice chairman Venu Srinivasan complained to the charity commissioner that SRTT's three permanent trustees were violating the law governing public trusts. SRTT had six trustees at the time.
 On 15 May, the charity commissioner ordered that the Trust could not hold meetings or take decisions while an investigation was under way. The order was issued without giving Tata Trusts an opportunity to explain its position, the charitable organizations had said then in a statement.
 The amendment has fuelled confusion because it does not clearly state whether its restrictions apply only to appointments made after 1 September 2025 or also to existing appointments.
 Tata Trusts maintains that the amendment is prospective and does not affect appointments made before it came into force. It says all three of SRTT's perpetual trustees—Noel Tata, Jimmy Tata and Jehangir HC Jehangir—were appointed before the amendment.
 “It is the understanding of the Tata Trusts that the said amendment is prospective in nature and does not affect the appointments of perpetual trustees made prior to its coming into force on 1st September 2025. This is substantiated by both opinions and clarifications obtained by the Tata Trusts,” Tata Trusts said in a statement on the evening of 15 May.
 Deadlock spreads to Tata Sons 
 The paralysis at SRTT has had consequences beyond the trust itself. Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT), which owns 27.98% of Tata Sons, and SRTT, which owns 23.56%, are the two principal Tata Trusts. Together with smaller trusts, they hold 65.9% of the company.
 Tata Sons' rules require representatives of both SDTT and SRTT to be present for a general meeting to proceed. With SRTT unable to take decisions or send representatives, Tata Sons' AGM was adjourned on 18 August for lack of quorum.
 The impasse has also prevented shareholders from resolving a separate disagreement over Tata Sons' leadership.
 Noel Tata, chairman of Tata Trusts, was outvoted by the Tata Sons board on 17 September,

News 
 State-run bank chiefs see credit growth holding firm despite margin pressures
 Harsh Kumar 5 min read 2 Nov 2026, 12:01 PM IST 
 Summary
 Rising funding costs and competition for deposits remain key challenges. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 New Delhi: Six state-run banks have signalled confidence in credit growth in the second half of FY27 even as they face pressure on net interest margins (NIM) from deposit costs and competitive funding conditions. 
 Strong demand from retail, agriculture, micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and companies, along with festive-season borrowing, is expected to support loan growth, while foreign currency non-resident (bank), or FCNR (B), deposits have provided lenders with an additional source of funding, the chiefs of Punjab National Bank, Bank of Baroda, Canara Bank, Indian Bank, Indian Overseas Bank and Uco Bank said in interviews to Mint . 
 The Indian banking sector is navigating a trade-off between protecting profitability and sustaining loan growth, with festive demand expected to provide an additional boost. Together, the six lenders hold deposits of ₹ 64.5 trillion, which accounts for about 41% of the total public sector bank deposit base of ₹ 156.3 trillion.
 While floating-rate loans are repriced relatively quickly, deposit costs tend to adjust with a lag. Competition for term deposits and the need to sustain funding momentum could weigh on margins in the coming quarters. However, bank managements are not signaling any broad-based slowdown in credit demand, with growth estimates ranging from 11% to 15%. 
 However, rising funding costs and competition for deposits remain key challenges. Uco Bank managing director and chief executive officer in-charge Rajendra Kumar Saboo identified current account and savings account mobilization as a concern, citing changing savings and investment patterns among customers. 
 Canara Bank flagged the potential mark-to-market impact of rising government security yields, which have increased from 6.75% in June to 7.38%.
 Despite these pressures, the bank chiefs remain confident about sustaining loan growth, supported by improving asset quality, resilient domestic demand and alternative funding sources. Maintaining a balance between deposit costs and lending yields will remain central to profitability in the second half of FY27. 
 Punjab National Bank 
 Punjab National Bank MD and CEO Ashok Chandra expects the lender's credit growth to remain at 14-15% in the coming quarters, supported by retail, agriculture and MSME lending. Its domestic NIM increased 10 basis points sequentially to 2.74% in the September quarter. Chandra expects the recent 25-basis-point repo rate increase alone to contribute an additional seven basis points to margins. 
 PNB’s MSME portfolio growth is expected to accelerate to 21-22%, while agriculture lending is projected to grow 18-19%. PNB mobilized $2.7 billion through FCNR (B) deposits and has deployed the amount to replace bulk deposits and certificates of deposit, helping reduce funding costs. 
 Canara Bank is looking to sustain its credit growth momentum, supported by retail demand and improving asset quality. Its advances grew 18% year-on-year, while total business expanded by more than 14%, MD and CEO Brajesh Kumar Singh said. The bank has retained its FY27 advance growth guidance of 11-12%. 
 Canara Bank's retail portfolio grew 31.6% year-on-year, with housing and vehicle loans expected to remain key drivers during the festive season. Singh said the bank did not expect margins to shrink, citing its underwriting standards and low fresh slippages. 
 Canara Bank mobilized $5.8 billion through FCNR (B) deposits, equivalent to about ₹ 55,000 crore. Singh described these deposits, with tenures of three to five years, as a stable funding source, adding that their cost was around 100 basis points below prevailing market benchmarks. They are exempt from cash reserve ratio and statutory liquidity ratio requirements. 
 Indian Bank raised its FY27 advance growth guidance to 13-14% from 11-13% earlier, while increasing its deposit growth outlook to 11-12% from 9-11%. Advances grew 16.4% year-on-year to ₹ 7.22 trillion as of 30 September, while deposits increased 12.5% to ₹ 8.74 trillion. 
 Indian Bank 
 Indian Bank MD and CEO Binod Kumar said retail advances grew 17.37%, agriculture advances increased 17.18% and MSME lending expanded 19.06% year-on-year. Indian Bank collected $2.3 billion through FCNR deposits and another $400 million through overseas foreign currency borrowings until 30 September. It raised $500 million through external commercial borrowings and expects to raise another $500 million by December. 
 Uco Bank raised $730 million, comprising $630 million of FCNR (B) deposits and $100 million through other foreign currency deposits. Bank chief Saboo said the additional liquidity supported lending requirements and helped the bank avoid raising fresh bulk deposits at higher interest rates. Advances grew 24.7% year-on-year in the September quarter, significantly higher than its full-year guidance of 12-14%.
 Uco Bank reported a global NIM of 3% in the September quarter, above its FY27 guidance of 2.8-2.9%. Saboo expects margins to remain above the guidance, supported by the repricing of loans linked to the external benchmark lending rate following the repo rate increase. 
 IOB mobilized ₹ 11,000 crore, equivalent to $1.12 billion, through FCNR (B) deposits. MD and CEO Ajay Kumar Srivastava said the rupee equivalent had been deployed in lending. 
 The bank's global advances grew 24.35% year-on-year to ₹ 3.46 trillion as of 30 September, while deposits increased 20.16% to ₹ 4.07 trillion. Its domestic NIM stood at 3.49% in the September quarter, compared with 3.48% in June. Srivastava expects margins across the banking sector to improve by 3-5 basis points.

News 
 SC rebuke in Vedanta dispute exposes gaps in India’s fast-track arbitration push
 Krishna Yadav 5 min read 2 Nov 2026, 12:59 PM IST 
 Summary
 The apex court's sharp criticism of the Centre over a 22-year-old Ravva oilfield dispute highlights how state-led litigation and enforcement delays continue to undermine India's global arbitration ambitions. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 India’s ambitions to establish itself as a global arbitration hub face persistent challenges due to prolonged state-driven litigation and institutional delays. Repeated Supreme Court criticism over extended challenges to enforcement orders, frequently driven by state entities, underscores the stark gap between India’s push for fast-track dispute resolution and its actual implementation. 
 These systemic shortcomings were brought into sharp focus on Monday as the Supreme Court sharply criticised the Union government for prolonging a dispute involving a 22-year-old arbitral award in favour of mining major Vedanta Ltd, saying its approach was frustrating the enforcement of an arbitration decision. 
 A bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and Manmohan dismissed the Centre’s appeal against a Delhi High Court order allowing Vedanta and Ravva Oil (Singapore) Pvt Ltd to enforce foreign arbitral awards in the Ravva oilfield dispute.
 “You are frustrating an arbitral award like this at the stage of enforcement. We talk about arbitration , the seat and all this. Nobody will trust you,” the bench told the Centre’s counsel during the hearing.
 The bench said it found no error, much less an error of law, in the Delhi High Court’s 1 July 2026 judgment. It observed that the high court had considered all relevant aspects of the matter and passed a correct order. 
 The Supreme Court’s rebuke adds to its recurring criticism of prolonged challenges to arbitral awards and delays in their enforcement, particularly involving government entities. 
 Last week, the apex court asked the Law Commission to examine the framework for enforcing arbitral awards and recommend measures to expedite their execution. The direction came while hearing a separate dispute involving Royal Construction Company and National Projects Construction Corporation, in which parties were still litigating over enforcement more than 24 years after a 2002 arbitral award. 
 In May 2026, while dismissing a challenge by the Madhya Pradesh Road Development Corporation to an arbitral award in favour of Jabalpur Corridor Pvt Ltd, the Supreme Court observed that “the government’s role cannot be ignored” in undermining arbitration. It also said, “Arbitration in India has not failed; however, courts sometimes have failed arbitration in India.” 
 The latest remarks come as India seeks to position itself as an international arbitration hub through legal and institutional reforms. Amendments to the Arbitration and Conciliation Act in 2015, 2019 and 2020 sought to reduce court intervention and expedite proceedings. The government also established the India International Arbitration Centre (IIAC) in 2019 and provided for an Arbitration Council of India to grade arbitral institutions and promote professional standards. 
 However, the government told Parliament in February 2026 that the council was yet to be constituted. A parliamentary panel report in August 2026 also noted that the IIAC had handled only 17 cases in nearly three years, highlighting the gap between India's arbitration ambitions and institutional progress. 
 ‘Credibility at stake’
 According to lawyers, the Supreme Court’s remarks expose deeper gaps in India’s arbitration framework, particularly prolonged challenges by government bodies.
 Tushar Kumar, advocate, Supreme Court of India, said the observation was a warning about India’s credibility as an arbitration destination. “The state, being the largest commercial litigant in the country, bears a heightened institutional responsibility to demonstrate fidelity to the rule of law and respect for the finality of adjudicatory outcomes,” he said. He attributed prolonged challenges partly to bureaucratic risk aversion, with officials often fearing scrutiny for accepting adverse awards.
 Shiv Sapra, partner at Kochhar & Co, said, “The government cannot champion arbitration as a matter of policy while frustrating its outcomes through litigation.” He called for time-bound enforcement, meaningful costs for frivolous challenges, and accountability for avoidable delays, adding, “India cannot aspire to become a global arbitration hub while allowing enforcement to become a second round of litigation.”
 The Ravva dispute 
 The dispute stems from a 1994 production-sharing contract between the government and a consortium comprising ONGC , Videocon Petroleum, Ravva Oil and Cairn Energy to develop the Ravva oilfield in the Krishna-Godavari basin. Cairn India, which later merged with Vedanta, was part of the consortium.
 The dispute centred on how payments towards ONGC ’s historical costs should be accounted for while calculating the parties’ respective revenue shares from oil production. This came to be known as the ONGC Carry issue. The contract provided for arbitration in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. 
 In a partial award dated 12 October 2004, the tribunal ruled in favour of the companies on two of six issues and in favour of the government on the remaining four, leaving the quantification of the ONGC Carry issue to be determined later. 
 The government subsequently challenged the partial award before Malaysian courts, but it was ultimately upheld by the country's Federal Court in October 2011. 
 In July 2014, the government issued show-cause notices seeking $64 million from Vedanta and $35 million from Ravva Oil, threatening to recover the amounts from proceeds payable to the companies from oil sales. The companies returned to the tribunal to resolve the outstanding quantifi

News 
 Prosus looks to strengthen India bets on platforms and marketplaces
 Sneha Shah , Mansi Verma 4 min read 3 Nov 2026, 06:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 The technology-focused investment firm, which recently infused $100 million in Sachin Bansal’s fintech platform Navi, is looking to deepen its financial services thesis, Ashutosh Sharma, India head at Prosus, told Mint in an interview. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Amsterdam-based Prosus is looking to invest in companies with platform or marketplace-led business models as it seeks to deepen its presence in India's financial services sector and other consumer-facing businesses, a senior company executive said.
 The technology-focused investment firm, which recently infused $100 million in Sachin Bansal’s fintech platform Navi, is looking to deepen its financial services thesis, Ashutosh Sharma, India head at Prosus, told Mint in an interview.
 Last week, the Competition Commission of India (CCI) approved Prosus's $100 million (around ₹ 940 crore) investment in Navi for an 8.5% stake. The entirely primary investment, one of the first institutional capital infusions into the company, values Navi at more than ₹ 13,000 crore.
 Prosus counts companies such as PayU, Vastu Finance, Mintifi and GrowXCD, among others, as part of its financial services portfolio. However, consumer-facing fintech was a missing piece [until the Navi deal], said Sharma.
 “If you look at the gaps in our portfolio, most consumer categories are spoken for. In food, we have something; in quick commerce, we have something; in mobility, we now have Rapido; in travel, we have an OTA (online travel agency) through Ixigo; in e-commerce, we have Meesho; and in services, we have Urban Company. But one big gap was a consumer-facing fintech platform. PayU is in our portfolio, and we own all of PayU, but it is largely a B2B payments and B2B credit business. So, a B2C fintech platform was a missing piece in our portfolio,” Sharma said.
 Founded in 2018 by Flipkart co-founder Sachin Bansal, Navi offers UPI, credit, insurance and broking services through a single platform. For the financial year ended 31 March 2026, its operating revenue rose 16.2% year-on-year to ₹ 2,981.7 crore. The company reported a consolidated net loss of ₹ 466 crore in FY26, compared with ₹ 126.4 crore in FY25, according to Tracxn data.
 Navi Finserv, the group’s lending arm, had assets under management (AUM) of ₹ 13,138 crore in FY26, which have already risen to over ₹ 23,440 crore by the middle of this year.
 “The interesting thing is that it is not a monoline business. It is a multiline business. They (Navi) have a UPI business, credit, brokerage and insurance. In that sense, it is truly a platform,” Sharma said, adding that the company operates in a large market with significant platform potential.
 Platforms over single-product businesses
 Prosus prefers businesses that operate as platforms or marketplaces, rather than companies offering a single product or service.
 “We have a very big affinity for platforms and marketplaces. Swiggy is that, Meesho is that, Rapido is that, Urban Company is that, and Ixigo is that. These types of businesses, which are platforms or marketplaces, we understand and appreciate slightly more,” Sharma said.
 The investment philosophy is also reflected in Prosus’s portfolio construction. The firm, which has access to patient, long-term capital, has built concentrated positions in companies across sectors rather than spreading its investments thinly.
 Its investment in Rapido is one example. Prosus first invested $180 million in the mobility platform in April 2022, when it was valued at $1.1 billion. Swiggy has since fully exited its ₹ 2,400 crore stake in Rapido, selling shares to Prosus and WestBridge Capital. The transaction values Rapido at around $2.5-2.7 billion, delivering nearly 2.5 times returns on Prosus’s initial investment in just over three years.
 Long-term bets, IPO-ready firms
 Sharma said Prosus believes India’s economic growth offers a long runway for its portfolio companies, making it worthwhile to maintain sizeable positions even as some of them enter public markets.
 “If you look at GDP per capita growth or overall GDP growth in our country, despite all the headwinds around war,fuel prices and so on, I think we are growing at a very decent clip. If, for a moment, we assume that some of these global macroeconomic and geopolitical challenges don’t exist, I think we have the opportunity to grow at this pace for many years to come, probably decades," he said.
 “Therefore, in my view, across most of our companies, even if they are listed, it is quite early in their earnings journey. Having concentrated positions in these companies allows us to ride this growth wave that our country presents for a few years, if not a few decades, in a meaningful way.”
 Rapido, Vastu Finance, PayU and Navi are among the late-stage companies in Prosus’s India portfolio, several of which could potentially tap the public markets as they scale.
 “There is no pressure from us. But I think at least three or four companies are ready from that standpoint. When they decide to pull the trigger is something I don’t know,” Sharma said.

docs.title: There may be a new 'Fragile Five'—and they're all among the most developed economies in the world
docs.text:
Opinion 
 There may be a new 'Fragile Five'—and they're all among the most developed economies in the world
 Narayan Ramachandran 4 min read 2 Nov 2026, 04:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 These countries are worthy of being called the new Fragile Five. Not in the same economic sense of currency weakness and debt default, but in terms of societal unrest. Here's why. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 During an economic milestone event in 2013 called the “taper tantrum,” a Morgan Stanley analyst coined the term “Fragile Five.” Turkey, Brazil, India, South Africa and Indonesia were counted among them because they faced declining currencies, soaring bond yields, high inflation and large external debt burdens, which were insufficiently covered by their local reserves. This fragility was manifest when extremely low global interest rates were “tapered” back towards normalcy. 
 Today’s Fragile Five belong entirely to the Group of Seven (G7) countries, which are the most developed in the world. The Fragile Five in 2026 are France, Italy, the UK, Germany and the US. And they are fragile not only in economic terms but also in a societal context. 
 As interest rates have normalized around the world after covid and the stagnation of the 2010s decade, developed markets with high debt loads have felt the impact. 
 These democracies had piled on the debt to cushion the impact of both crises, but rising interest rates have increased debt service costs and rising inflation has caused government expenditure to rise at the same time. 
 This has the effect of expanding the primary deficit and the fiscal deficit at the same time. Add to this toxic economic cocktail the dramatic increase in oil prices, and you have the makings not only of economic distress but also social unrest. 
 No country today reflects this fragility more than France. Student protests ostensibly triggered by school conditions in Paris’s poor northern suburbs have widened into a cost-of-living revolt. 
 These student-led protests are being held in the backdrop of France having a fiscal deficit of over 5% of gross domestic product (GDP), unemployment at 8.3% and high fuel prices. 
 In France, these protests are eerily reminiscent of the May ’68 riots. Those riots from nearly six decades ago scarred and polarized France. What began as student protests then morphed into a general strike with over 11 million workers joining in. 
 The widespread rioting, police action and eventual general election left an indelible mark on French society. The degree of street violence was very high. Now, as then, the police has been accused of using a heavy-handed approach to containing the riots. 
 There are differences too. Unlike now, France in 1968 was in the late stage of an economic boom widely referred to as Les Trente Glorieuses (the glorious thirty) post-war years. While both protests were student-led, the proximate cause for the May ’68 protests were university conditions. 
 The earlier riots moved rapidly from Nanterre University to the wealthy left bank of the Seine in Paris. Today’s riots were catalysed in the disadvantaged areas surrounding Saint-Denis and are clearly sparked by economic angst among those less well-off in France. 
 Conservatives in France have always considered the May ’68 riots as left-wing protests. They think so of today’s riots too, but more neutrally they are cross-ideological and anti-establishment in character. 
 The other four countries—the UK, Italy, Germany and the US—embody some of France’s fragility syndrome. UK has a budget deficit of 4% of GDP, unemployment of 5% and inflation of 3.1%. Because of this evolving fragility, the UK has had seven prime ministers in the last 10 years. One of them, Liz Truss, lasted only 49 days, forced out when her budget included unfunded tax cuts that sparked a meltdown in its gilt market. 
 While smaller than France’s, Italy had its worst unrest over cost-of-living since mid-October, with clashes and looting in several northern Italian cities and fuel-price blockades in the south. Italy’s debt-to-GDP is 140% and its unemployment is 5.7%. 
 In the US, President Donald Trump is the least popular president at the mid-term point in eight decades. There are many reasons for this, but affordability and inflation top the list. The US federal government debt has crossed $40 trillion, total local and federal debt-related budget deficit is now nearly 8% of GDP and total debt-to-GDP is about 126% (20% higher than the immediate post-World War II peak). 
 Germany, though fragile, is the least at risk of the five. German debt-to-GDP is still well under 100% and its fiscal deficit is only a bit higher than the Maastricht-established norm of 3%. Despite this, Germany’s Gen Z has issued a call for a protest planned soon. 
 Beyond the G7, Belgium with a 5% of GDP fiscal deficit and Spain with 10% unemployment have already seen street protests and would qualify in the “fragile” category. 
 Developed democracies cushioned their societies from the ill-effects of the global financial crisis and covid with massive fiscal spending. Real incomes, youth jobs and public services lagged after the cushion ended. 
 As interest rates have normalized, and fears of artificial intelligence taking away jobs has grown, five of them—France, Italy, the UK, US and Germany—are worthy of being called the new Fragile Five. Not in the same economic sense of currency weakness (their currencies are free and floating) and debt default but in terms of societal unrest. 
 The G7 fiscal scaffolding is showing its weakness as the Strait of Hormuz-related oil price shock manifests in the same way as external vulnerability manifested itself for emerging markets when extremely low rates were normalized through the taper. 
 P.S: “He who slings mud generally loses ground,” said American diplomat Adlai Stevenson. 
 The author is chairman, InKlude L

docs.title: Trump surprises Republicans with election eve speech about reflecting pool
